## Double-Entry Bookkeeping Basics
Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction in at least two accounts, ensuring the books always balance. The golden rule is that for every debit, there must be an equal and offsetting credit.
To record a transaction, first identify it: determine if cash is moving in or out and which category it belongs to (e.g., inventory purchase, sales revenue, rent expense). Then determine the two accounts affected, such as 'Inventory' and 'Cash' when paying for inventory with cash.
Apply the debit and credit rules using the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity). Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue. Record the entry with the date, description, debit amount, and credit amount in the general ledger, then verify that total debits equal total credits.

## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere. They move by mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, with relative motion measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries involve collision and thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Transform boundaries have plates sliding past, producing strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths.
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Pre-existing faults concentrate slip, cold brittle lithosphere borders warm ductile mantle focusing deformation, and curved margins force localized shear zones. Thus, earthquakes are not random; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.

At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, producing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. At convergent boundaries, plates collide, causing thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. ## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, meaning they follow the movement patterns of tectonic plates. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, and their relative motion is measured in centimeters per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At plate boundaries, earthquakes cluster because of four main reasons. Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Different boundary types produce different seismic styles. Divergent boundaries (plates pull apart) cause normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries (plates collide) cause thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow. Transform boundaries (plates slide past) cause strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate.

## Types of Plate Boundaries
The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere. Plates move due to mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, with relative motion measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, producing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. At convergent boundaries, plates collide, causing thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other, generating strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths.
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges are locked by friction, causing strain to build until it exceeds rock strength. Pre-existing faults, rheological contrasts, and geometric incompatibility also focus deformation. Thus, earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.

## Bismarck's Alliance System
After Germany unified in 1871, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck aimed to keep the new Reich secure by isolating France, which resented its defeat and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. He managed crises like the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and built alliances: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882, and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France allied with Russia in 1894, creating the threat of a two-front war for Germany.
Britain ended its 'splendid isolation' through the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Entente in 1907, settling colonial disputes. These agreements had no formal military obligations, but by 1907 Europe was split into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, turning local quarrels into continental issues.
An arms race accompanied the realignment. German naval laws of 1898 and 1900, pushed by Admiral Tirpitz, challenged British sea power, and HMS Dreadnought in 1906 intensified battleship rivalry. The Schlieffen Plan of 1905 committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium. Military spending rose after 1900, and general staffs gained influence.
Crises eroded trust: the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) ended in German humiliation at Algeciras; Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia in 1908 forced Russia to back down; the Agadir Crisis of 1911 brought France and Germany to the brink of war.

## The Triple Alliance and Reinsurance Treaty
After Germany unified in 1871, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck worked to keep France isolated because France resented its defeat and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. He built alliances to protect the new German Reich. In 1879, Germany made the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, and Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance. In 1887, Bismarck also made the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to keep Russia neutral.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France saw a chance and formed the Franco-Russian Alliance in 1894. This meant Germany could face a war on two fronts. Britain also changed its policy of staying isolated. The Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Entente in 1907 created the Triple Entente, even though these agreements had no formal military duties. By 1907, Europe was split into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
An arms race grew alongside the diplomatic split. Germany's naval laws of 1898 and 1900, pushed by Admiral Tirpitz, challenged Britain's sea power, and Britain's HMS Dreadnought in 1906 made the battleship race worse. On land, the Schlieffen Plan of 1905 committed Germany to a quick attack on France through Belgium. Military spending rose after 1900, and generals gained more influence over foreign policy.
Crises made trust between the blocs worse. In the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06), Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to challenge French influence, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 humiliated Germany. In 1908, Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angering Serbia and forcing Russia to back down. The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off Morocco, nearly caused war between France and Germany.

## The Water Cycle
The water cycle, also called the hydrologic cycle, is driven by solar energy, which heats oceans and causes evaporation. Water moves through different states—liquid, gas (vapor), and solid (ice)—and is stored in reservoirs: oceans (97%), ice caps, groundwater, and the atmosphere (small but fast turnover).
Key processes include evaporation (water to vapor), transpiration (plants releasing water), condensation (cloud formation), precipitation (rain/snow), and runoff/infiltration (water returning to oceans or ground). The cycle is a closed system: the total mass of water stays the same, only its location and state change.
In contrast, the carbon cycle is a chemical cycle involving chemical changes, not just physical state changes. Its reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, ocean (dissolved CO2), biosphere, and atmosphere. Processes include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, and diffusion.

## The Carbon Cycle
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, unlike the water cycle which involves physical state changes. It moves carbon through reservoirs: rocks (especially sedimentary), fossil fuels, the ocean (as dissolved CO2), the biosphere (plants and animals), and the atmosphere (as CO2 and CH4).
Key processes include photosynthesis, where plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen, drawing carbon down. Respiration releases CO2 when living things break down glucose. Decomposition releases carbon from dead matter. Combustion of fossil fuels or trees releases large amounts of carbon into the atmosphere. Diffusion exchanges CO2 between the ocean and air.

## Comparing Water and Carbon Cycles
The biggest difference between the water and carbon cycles is that water mostly undergoes phase changes (liquid, gas, solid), while carbon undergoes chemical transformations that change its bonds, such as in photosynthesis and combustion. This is the key point to remember for the final exam.
Carbon is an element, while water is a compound. The carbon cycle includes a gas phase, with carbon dioxide and methane as gases.
Water moves through its cycle quickly, with days or weeks in the atmosphere, while carbon can be trapped for millions of years in limestone or coal, or move quickly through respiration.
The sun drives the water cycle, while life and geological processes drive the carbon cycle. Human activities affect both: dams, irrigation, and pollution affect water, while burning fossil fuels affects carbon, leading to the greenhouse effect.

Carbon is an element, while water is a compound. This is a key distinction: elements are made of one type of atom, compounds of two or more.

## The Carbon Cycle
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, unlike the water cycle which involves physical state changes. It moves carbon through reservoirs: rocks (especially sedimentary), fossil fuels, the ocean (as dissolved CO2), the biosphere (plants and animals), and the atmosphere (as CO2 and CH4).
Key processes include photosynthesis, where plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen, drawing carbon down. Respiration releases CO2 when living things break down glucose. Decomposition releases carbon from dead matter. Combustion of fossil fuels or trees releases large amounts of carbon into the atmosphere. Diffusion exchanges CO2 between the ocean and air.

## Comparing Water and Carbon Cycles
The biggest difference between the water and carbon cycles is that water mostly undergoes phase changes (liquid, gas, solid), while carbon undergoes chemical transformations that change its bonds, such as in photosynthesis and combustion. This is the key point to remember for the final exam.
Carbon is an element, while water is a compound. The carbon cycle includes a gas phase, with carbon dioxide and methane as gases.
Water moves through its cycle quickly, with days or weeks in the atmosphere, while carbon can be trapped for millions of years in limestone or coal, or move quickly through respiration.
The sun drives the water cycle, while life and geological processes drive the carbon cycle. Human activities affect both: dams, irrigation, and pollution affect water, while burning fossil fuels affects carbon, leading to the greenhouse effect.

## Interconnections Between Cycles
Carbon is an element, while water is a compound.
The biggest difference between the cycles is that carbon involves chemical bonding changes (like photosynthesis and combustion), whereas water is mostly phase changes (liquid, gas, solid). Water is phase-change heavy; carbon is transformation-heavy.

Every bill introduced in the Assembly must have a Sponsor and at least two Seconders. The Sponsor is the Delegate who files the bill, and the Seconders are other Delegates who support it.

Committees meet in Room 114 during the Thursday Activity Block. A quorum of five members is required. The committee may report the bill favorably, report it with amendments, table it until the next calendar month, or kill it by a two-thirds vote of members present.

The most important rule is that no bill can be voted on the same day it gets its Second Reading, unless every Delegate present agrees to it. This rule is stressed heavily, so it is a key point to remember.
After the Second Reading, amendments are voted on one by one, by a show of hands, before the final vote on the bill. The Third Reading happens right after the amendments are settled, and the bill passes if it gets a simple majority of Delegates present, but at least eleven yes votes.

## Dosing of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Carvedilol and labetalol additionally block α1 receptors, leading to vasodilation.
Typical adult doses are once-daily unless noted. Metoprolol tartrate is 50–100 mg twice daily; ER is 25–200 mg once daily. Atenolol 25–100 mg, bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg, nebivolol 2.5–20 mg. Carvedilol 3.125–25 mg twice daily (titrate). Propranolol IR 40–160 mg three or four times daily, or LA 80–160 mg once daily. Sotalol 80–160 mg twice daily, adjust for renal function.
Renal excretion: atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol require dose adjustment when CrCl <30 mL/min. Half-lives vary: metoprolol 3–7 h (ER 12 h), bisoprolol 10–12 h, carvedilol 7–10 h, nebivolol 12–20 h. Oral bioavailability: metoprolol 50%, atenolol 50%, propranolol 30% (high first-pass).

## Indications for β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective drugs (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective drugs (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Mixed α/β blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add α1-blockade for vasodilation.
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) using bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, or nebivolol. They also control rate in AF/flutter, prevent ventricular arrhythmias (sotalol), and treat migraine (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).
Typical adult doses are once-daily unless noted: metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg bid, ER 25–200 mg; atenolol 25–100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg; carvedilol 3.125–25 mg bid; nebivolol 2.5–20 mg; propranolol 40–160 mg tid/qid (IR) or 80–160 mg LA; sotalol 80–160 mg bid. Adjust renally excreted drugs (atenolol, nadolol, sotalol) for CrCl <30 mL/min.

## Contraindications and cautions
β-blockers are contraindicated in asthma, bradycardia, heart block, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure. In asthma, avoid non-selective agents. In decompensated HF, initiate only when the patient is euvolemic.
Cautions include pregnancy (avoid atenolol, prefer labetalol), diabetes (can mask hypoglycemia, prefer β1-selective or nebivolol), and severe peripheral arterial disease (risk of ischemia).
Key interactions: digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, ivabradine increase bradycardia; ACEi/ARB and diuretics increase hypotension; NSAIDs reduce antihypertensive effect; CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) raise metoprolol levels.
Monitoring includes HR, BP, ECG, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and lipids. Withdrawal should be tapered over 1–2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia and ischemia.

## Monitoring and adverse effects
Beta-blockers require monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure, ECG intervals, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and lipids. Non-selective agents can raise triglycerides and lower HDL.
Adverse effects range from common fatigue, cold extremities, and sexual dysfunction to less common bronchospasm, masked hypoglycemia, depression, and heart block.
Avoid in asthma with reversible bronchospasm, bradycardia below 50 bpm, second/third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, and severe peripheral arterial disease.
In pregnancy, avoid atenolol due to IUGR; labetalol is preferred. In diabetes, prefer beta-1 selective agents or nebivolol to reduce masking of hypoglycemia.
Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia; taper over 1-2 weeks. In elderly, start low and go slow; in CKD, reduce doses of renally cleared agents like atenolol and nadolol.

## Withdrawal and special populations
Stopping a beta-blocker suddenly can cause rebound tachycardia, high blood pressure, and ischemia. To avoid this, taper the dose over 1–2 weeks.
In elderly patients, start with a low dose and increase slowly. In chronic kidney disease (CKD), use renally cleared agents like atenolol or nadolol with dose reduction.
In heart failure, beta-blockers are uptitrated to target doses, such as bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, or metoprolol-ER 200 mg.

## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere. They move by mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, with relative motion measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries involve collision and thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. Transform boundaries have plates sliding past, producing strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths.
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Pre-existing faults concentrate slip, cold brittle lithosphere borders warm ductile mantle focusing deformation, and curved margins force localized shear zones. Thus, earthquakes are not random; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, meaning they follow the movement patterns of tectonic plates. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, and their relative motion is measured in centimeters per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At plate boundaries, earthquakes cluster because of four main reasons. Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Different boundary types produce different seismic styles. Divergent boundaries (plates pull apart) cause normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries (plates collide) cause thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow. Transform boundaries (plates slide past) cause strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, meaning they follow the movement patterns of tectonic plates. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, and their relative motion is measured in centimeters per year (cm yr⁻¹).
At plate boundaries, earthquakes cluster because of four main reasons. Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Different boundary types produce different seismic styles. Divergent boundaries (plates pull apart) cause normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Convergent boundaries (plates collide) cause thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow. Transform boundaries (plates slide past) cause strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate.

## The Water Cycle
The water cycle, also called the hydrologic cycle, is driven by solar energy, which heats oceans and causes evaporation. Water moves through different states—liquid, gas (vapor), and solid (ice)—and is stored in reservoirs: oceans (97%), ice caps, groundwater, and the atmosphere (small but fast turnover).
Key processes include evaporation (water to vapor), transpiration (plants releasing water), condensation (cloud formation), precipitation (rain/snow), and runoff/infiltration (water returning to oceans or ground). The cycle is a closed system: the total mass of water stays the same, only its location and state change.
In contrast, the carbon cycle is a chemical cycle involving chemical changes, not just physical state changes. Its reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, ocean (dissolved CO2), biosphere, and atmosphere. Processes include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, and diffusion.

Key: Water cycle involves physical state changes; carbon cycle involves chemical changes.
Key: Water cycle is a closed system with constant mass.

## The Carbon Cycle
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, unlike the water cycle which involves physical state changes. It moves carbon through reservoirs: rocks (especially sedimentary), fossil fuels, the ocean (as dissolved CO2), the biosphere (plants and animals), and the atmosphere (as CO2 and CH4).
Key processes include photosynthesis, where plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen, drawing carbon down. Respiration releases CO2 when living things break down glucose. Decomposition releases carbon from dead matter. Combustion of fossil fuels or trees releases large amounts of carbon into the atmosphere. Diffusion exchanges CO2 between the ocean and air.

## Comparing Water and Carbon Cycles
The biggest difference between the water and carbon cycles is that water mostly undergoes phase changes (liquid, gas, solid), while carbon undergoes chemical transformations that change its bonds, such as in photosynthesis and combustion. This is the key point to remember for the final exam.
Carbon is an element, while water is a compound. The carbon cycle includes a gas phase, with carbon dioxide and methane as gases.
Water moves through its cycle quickly, with days or weeks in the atmosphere, while carbon can be trapped for millions of years in limestone or coal, or move quickly through respiration.
The sun drives the water cycle, while life and geological processes drive the carbon cycle. Human activities affect both: dams, irrigation, and pollution affect water, while burning fossil fuels affects carbon, leading to the greenhouse effect.

## Assembly Composition and Officers

## Quorum and Session Rules
The Assembly has 31 elected Delegates. The Speaker presides and votes only to break ties. The Clerk keeps the Ledger of Bills, and the Provost of Finance certifies spending bills.

The Speaker refers each bill to one of four standing committees: Grounds (7), Clubs (7), Chest (9), or Rules (8). A bill spending more than 40 Silver Marks must go to the Committee on the Chest.

## Bill Introduction and Filing
Any Delegate may introduce a bill by filing three typed copies with the Clerk of the Roll before 8:15 a.m. on a Tuesday. The Clerk assigns a number with the prefix 'BA' followed by the session year, for example BA-24-07.
Every bill must have a Sponsor and at least two Seconders. The Clerk reads the title aloud at the first session after filing; this is the First Reading, and no debate occurs at that time.

## Sponsorship and First Reading
Every bill introduced in the Assembly must have a Sponsor and at least two Seconders. The Sponsor is the Delegate who files the bill, and the Seconders are other Delegates who support it.
To introduce a bill, a Delegate files three typed copies with the Clerk of the Roll before 8:15 a.m. on a Tuesday. The Clerk assigns a number with the prefix 'BA' and the session year.
At the first session after filing, the Clerk reads the bill's title aloud. This is called the First Reading. No debate occurs at the First Reading; it is simply a formal announcement.

The Speaker of Benches refers each bill to one of four standing committees: Grounds (7 members), Clubs (7 members), Chest (9 members), or Rules (8 members).

## Committee Meetings and Actions
Committees meet in Room 114 during the Thursday Activity Block. A quorum of five members is required. The committee may report the bill favorably, report it with amendments, table it until the next calendar month, or kill it by a two-thirds vote of members present.
After a bill is reported out, it receives its Second Reading no sooner than three school days later. The Clerk reads the full text. Delegates may speak once for up to four minutes; the Sponsor may speak twice.
Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote. The Third Reading occurs immediately after amendments are settled. Passage requires a simple majority of Delegates present, but never fewer than eleven yes votes.
No bill may be voted on the same day it receives its Second Reading, except by unanimous consent of all Delegates present.

## Second Reading and Debate
A bill that comes out of committee gets its Second Reading at least three school days later. At that reading, the Clerk reads the whole bill out loud, and each Delegate may speak once for up to four minutes, while the Sponsor may speak twice.
The most important rule is that no bill can be voted on the same day it gets its Second Reading, unless every Delegate present agrees to it. This rule is stressed heavily, so it is a key point to remember.
After the Second Reading, amendments are voted on one by one, by a show of hands, before the final vote on the bill. The Third Reading happens right after the amendments are settled, and the bill passes if it gets a simple majority of Delegates present, but at least eleven yes votes.

Key: Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote.

## Amendments and Third Reading
Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote. After all amendments are settled, the Third Reading occurs immediately. Passage requires a simple majority of Delegates present, but never fewer than eleven yes votes.

## Voting Day Restriction
The most important rule on voting day is that a bill cannot be voted on the same day it gets its Second Reading. The only exception is if every Delegate present agrees to it unanimously. This means that even if a majority wants to vote right away, they cannot unless everyone says yes.
Before the final vote, amendments are handled separately. Each amendment is voted on individually by a show of hands. After all amendments are settled, the Third Reading happens immediately, and then the final vote on the bill takes place.

Key: No bill may be voted on the same day it receives its Second Reading, except by unanimous consent of all Delegates present.

## Chancellor's Role and Signing
The Chancellor, elected at large, must act on a passed bill within five school days. The options are: sign it, making it an Act entered in the Ledger with a seal; veto it with a written objection of no more than 150 words; or return it unsigned after five days, in which case it becomes an Act without signature.

Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote. The Third Reading occurs immediately after amendments are settled. Passage requires a simple majority of Delegates present, but never fewer than eleven yes votes.

## Veto and Override
A vetoed bill returns to the floor at the next session. The Assembly may override the veto only by a vote of twenty-one of the thirty-one Delegates. If the override succeeds, the bill becomes an Act over the Chancellor's objection.
An Act takes effect at 8:00 a.m. on the tenth school day after signature, unless the Act itself states a later date. Acts affecting the Activity Chest take effect only after the Provost of Finance countersigns.
The Clerk of the Roll must publish every Act on the Assembly board within two school days of effect. Any Act not published within this window is suspended until publication occurs.
Repeal of an Act follows the same path as enactment, except that the committee stage may be waived by a two-thirds floor vote.
Emergency measures affecting health or safety may be introduced at any session and passed by a vote of twenty-four Delegates. Such measures expire automatically twenty school days after effect unless re-enacted under the ordinary procedure.

## Mechanism of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. There are three main types: β1-selective (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) which lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release; non-selective (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) which also block β2 receptors causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation; and mixed α/β (carvedilol, labetalol) which add α1-blockade leading to vasodilation.
Pharmacokinetics vary: oral bioavailability is 50% for metoprolol and atenolol, 30% for propranolol (high first-pass). Half-lives range from 3–7 h (metoprolol) to 12–20 h (nebivolol). Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol are renally excreted and need dose adjustment when CrCl <30 mL/min.
Typical adult doses are once-daily unless noted: metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg bid, ER 25–200 mg; atenolol 25–100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg; carvedilol 3.125–25 mg bid; nebivolol 2.5–20 mg; propranolol 40–160 mg tid/qid (IR) or 80–160 mg LA; sotalol 80–160 mg bid.
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, HFrEF (with bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), rate control in AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis (sotalol), migraine prophylaxis (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).
Key: Indications – Hypertension; chronic stable angina; post‑MI mortality reduction; HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol‑ER, nebivolol); rate control in AF/flutter; ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis
Key: Typical adult doses (once‑daily unless noted)

Q: Which β-blocker is most likely to cause bronchoconstriction due to β2 blockade? A: Propranolol. Propranolol is non-selective, blocking both β1 and β2, leading to bronchoconstriction.
Q: Which drug's dose must be adjusted in renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min)? A: Atenolol. Atenolol is renally excreted and requires dose adjustment.
Q: Which β-blocker is indicated for migraine prophylaxis? A: Propranolol. Propranolol is listed for migraine prophylaxis.
Q: A patient with HFrEF is prescribed a β-blocker. Which of the following is NOT one of the recommended agents? A: Atenolol. Atenolol is not listed among the HFrEF agents.
Q: Which β-blocker has the lowest oral bioavailability due to high first-pass metabolism? A: Propranolol. Propranolol has 30% bioavailability, the lowest listed.
Q: What is the typical once-daily dose range for bisoprolol? A: 1.25–10 mg. The dose range is given directly.

## Pharmacokinetics of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective drugs (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective drugs (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Carvedilol and labetalol add α1-blockade, leading to vasodilation.
Oral bioavailability varies: metoprolol and atenolol are 50%, propranolol is 30% due to high first-pass metabolism. ## Bismarck's Alliance System
After Germany unified in 1871, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck aimed to keep the new Reich secure by isolating France, which resented its defeat and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. He managed crises like the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and built alliances: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882, and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France allied with Russia in 1894, creating the threat of a two-front war for Germany.
Britain ended its 'splendid isolation' through the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Entente in 1907, settling colonial disputes. These agreements had no formal military obligations, but by 1907 Europe was split into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, turning local quarrels into continental issues.
An arms race accompanied the realignment. German naval laws of 1898 and 1900, pushed by Admiral Tirpitz, challenged British sea power, and HMS Dreadnought in 1906 intensified battleship rivalry. The Schlieffen Plan of 1905 committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium. Military spending rose after 1900, and general staffs gained influence.
Crises eroded trust: the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) ended in German humiliation at Algeciras; Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia in 1908 forced Russia to back down; the Agadir Crisis of 1911 brought France and Germany to the brink of war.

## The Triple Alliance and Reinsurance Treaty
After Germany unified in 1871, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck worked to keep France isolated because France resented its defeat and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. He built alliances to protect the new German Reich. In 1879, Germany made the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, and Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance. In 1887, Bismarck also made the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to keep Russia neutral.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France saw a chance and formed the Franco-Russian Alliance in 1894. This meant Germany could face a war on two fronts. Britain also changed its policy of staying isolated. The Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Entente in 1907 created the Triple Entente, even though these agreements had no formal military duties. By 1907, Europe was split into two armed camps: the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
An arms race grew alongside the diplomatic split. Germany's naval laws of 1898 and 1900, pushed by Admiral Tirpitz, challenged Britain's sea power, and Britain's HMS Dreadnought in 1906 made the battleship race worse. On land, the Schlieffen Plan of 1905 committed Germany to a quick attack on France through Belgium. Military spending rose after 1900, and generals gained more influence over foreign policy.
Crises made trust between the blocs worse. In the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06), Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to challenge French influence, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 humiliated Germany. In 1908, Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angering Serbia and forcing Russia to back down. The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off Morocco, nearly caused war between France and Germany.

The Balkan Wars of 1912-13 ended with the Treaty of London in May 1913 and the Treaty of Bucharest in August 1913. These treaties expelled the Ottoman Empire from Europe and left Serbia enlarged and victorious. Austria-Hungary saw this enlarged Serbia as an existential threat.
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb linked to the Black Hand, gave Vienna a pretext. Austria-Hungary's foreign minister, Count Leopold von Berchtold, secured from Germany a 'blank cheque'—an unconditional promise of support against Serbia—on 5-6 July.
The July Crisis unfolded rapidly. Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July, deliberately drafted to be unacceptable. Serbia's conciliatory reply of 25 July was rejected, and partial mobilisation began. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Tsar Nicholas II ordered general Russian mobilisation on 30 July, despite telegrams with Wilhelm II. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan required invading Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed by the Treaty of London of 1839. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.
Historians have debated responsibility. Fritz Fischer, in 'Griff nach der Weltmacht' (1961), argued German leaders deliberately sought European domination, reopening controversy after Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles. Most accounts now emphasise the interaction of alliance commitments, militarism, imperial rivalry, and Balkan nationalism, where decisions of individual statesmen turned a regional murder into a general European war.
